div.p: In this paper, a tradeoff between dynamic voltage scaling (DVS) techniques and faults tolerance is considered. With this purpose we realized and presented in the paper one heuristicbased DVS algorithm. The algorithm is realized for fault tolerant real-time systems where the fault tolerance is achieved running the task affected by a transient fault again using time redundancy. The goal of the presented algorithm is to find the voltage at which each task should be executed such that the energy consumed by the set of task is minimized. Beside energy minimization heuristic algorithm have to meet all fault tolerance constraint and all realtime requirements.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Power consumption is a major concern for many embedded systems. Dynamic voltage scaling (DVS), which adjusts the supply voltage and correspondingly the clock frequency dynamically, is known as one of the most effective low energy techniques for real-time systems (RTS) [1]. DVS exploits the quadratic relationship between CPU energy consumption and supply voltage. By lowering the supply voltage and correspondingly the clock frequency simultaneously, the energy consumption of processors can be reduced quadratically. Nowadays, DVS is a commonly used technique for energy management and is supported by many commercial processors [2].

In addition to low energy consumption, the fault tolerance is one of the most important issues in RTS design. All RTSs have been designed in order to be safe and extremely dependable [3]. Dependability can be affected by different kinds of faults, including transient, permanent and intermittent faults [4]. Among these, the transient faults are much more common than faults of other two types. Since transient faults have the feature that they occur and then disappear, fault tolerance can be achieved running the task affected by a transient fault again (i.e. reexecuting the task). It means that time redundancy can be used as fault tolerance techniques by exploiting free slack time in the system schedule to perform recovery executions, [5].

While time redundancy techniques use free slack time to improve dependability, DVS exploits slack time to decrease energy consumption. Because the free slack time is a limited resource, it is obvious that more slack time used for DVS leaves less time slack for fault tolerance, and vice versa. Therefore, there is a tradeoff between low energy consumption and high fault tolerance. This tradeoff is analyzed in several papers [6][7][8]. The common goal is to find the appropriate execution frequency for each real-time task so that the maximum energy saving is achieved for the given fault tolerance constraints.

The tradeoff between energy efficiency and faults tolerance is focus of this paper. In accordance with that, we designed a heuristic-based DVS algorithm for RTSs that attempts to minimize the energy consumed by a real-time task sets under fault tolerance constraints. Novelty of our approach is the use of response time analysis (RTA) to check the feasibility of fault tolerant real-time task sets [9].

We consider a scenario where a single CPU executes a set of periodic preemptable tasks. The operation voltage of the CPU may be switched between two or more valuesoption available in most modern computers, [2]. The problem we address in this paper is to assign the appropriate execution frequency to each real-time task so that real-time system is feasible under fault tolerance constraint and energy consumption is as minimal as possible.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents our notation and the underlying assumption. Next section III introduces our proposed heuristic-based algorithm. Section IV gives the simulation results and finally, section V presents our conclusions.

div.head: II. MODELS AND PROBLEM DESCRIPTION
div.p: We assume RTS composed of a set of n real-time tasks, Γ={τ 1 ,..., τ n } where each task τ i is defined by a minimum inter-arrival time T i , worst case execution time (WCET) C i , deadline D i and priority p i . We consider scenario where a single CPU executes a set of real-time tasks. Each task is assigned a unique priority and all of them are periodic, fully preemptive and independent. Algorithm for scheduling real-time tasks could be any priority assignment algorithm, [10].
The voltage and consequently the operating frequency of the CPU may be switched between m values, f j (j=1,..., m) where f j < f j+1 .

We also assume that faults can occur during execution of any task. We consider transient faults and assume that the consequences of a fault can be eliminated by simple reexecution of the affected task at its original priority level and at its original CPU frequency. div.p: The straightforward solution of the frequency assignment problem is to explicitly generate all n m frequency assignment vectors, reject unfeasible ones, and choose frequency assignment vector for which the power consumption of the task sets is minimal. The main difficulty of this approach is that it is too computationally intensive to be used for large task sets. Nevertheless, for small set of real-time tasks this algorithm is a useful and optimal solution.

div.head: III. PROPOSED HEURISTIC ALGORITHM
div.p: In order to solve large problem instances, we propose a heuristic algorithm to find near optimal solution of the frequency assignment problem in acceptable computational time. Figure 1 The algorithm starts from the frequency assignment vector F=(x m , x m , ..., x m ), which assigns the maximum execution frequency, f m , to each real-time task. Also, at the beginning, all tasks are allowed to change the frequencywe say that all tasks are unlocked.

An iteration of the algorithm decreases the frequency of one task for one frequency level. The chosen task is one for which the frequency decrement yields maximum power reduction among all unlocked tasks provided that task sets remains feasible.

To find such task, the algorithm checks any currently unlocked task, τ i . First, τ i 's frequency index is temporarily decreased for one frequency level, i.e. from x i to x i-1 , and the feasibility of task sets is tested using Eq. 2. If task sets is not feasible, τ i is locked. Otherwise, if task sets is feasible, the difference between power consumption of τ i at lower ( ) and higher ( ) frequency is calculated as

After that, the algorithm enters the next iteration. The algorithm finishes when there are no more unlocked tasks.
The frequency assignment vector containing frequency of locked tasks is the algorithm's output.

div.head: IV. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: We performed simulations with a number of synthesized real-time tasks sets and a few real-world applications. The input parameters of the simulations were realtime task sets characteristics (priority, deadline, period, and worst-case execution time), processor's voltage and frequency levels and fault constraints (minimum time interval between two consecutive faults).

In this section, we will present simulation results that relates to the task sets taken from the Generic Avionics Platform (GAP) case study, used in [11]. The parameters of this real-world application are summarized in Table I. The CPU model is based on Intel XScale PXA270 processor [2]. The data sheet of this processor is available online at its manufactures' websites. We used specifications listed in Table II.

The fault tolerance capability, presented by the minimum time interval between two consecutive faults (parameter T F ,) is assign value of 100ms. Figure 2 shows the reduction of power consumption achieved by the optimal frequency assignment algorithm (No.1 algorithm) and our proposed heuristic algorithm (No.2 algorithm) for five task sets created by taking first k, k=6,.., 10 tasks from GAP task set.

The x-axis represents the number of real-time tasks. The y-axis represents the power reduction calculated in percents. This reduction is presented as power saving with respect to the power consumption at maximum frequency.

The simulation shows that the proposed heuristic algorithm gives optimistic results. As can be seen from Fig. 1, the deviation of the heuristic algorithm with respect to the optimal frequency assignment approach is within the range of 0 to 3.5%. This deviation is very close to the optimal solution presented through the first algorithm (frequency assignment approach).

Generally, the heuristic algorithm is very fast. Even when applied to large real-time task sets (more than 30 tasks), the heuristic algorithm takes less then a couple of seconds to complete. On the other hand, No.1 algorithm takes several hours to generate the optimal solution for task sets with 10 or more tasks and a few frequency levels. It is obvious that it can not be applied on larger task sets.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In addition to being used by frequency and voltage scaling to save energy, the free slack time in RTSs can also be used in order to improve the fault tolerance. In this paper we have considered the problem of assigning the appropriate execution frequency to each real-time task so that fault tolerant RTS is feasible and that energy consumption is as minimal as possible. Fault tolerant constraint is represented by the minimum time interval between two consecutive faults that the RTS can tolerate. The free slack time, as the limited resource, causes the trade-off between the energy efficiency and the fault tolerance. Recognizing that this problem is NP-hard, we proposed a heuristic-based approach.

Our simulations results show that, in general, the proposed heuristic method can be practical solution for energy savings in fault tolerant RTSs. Indeed, the power reduction obtained by the heuristic algorithm is very close to the optimal frequency assignment for large real-time task sets and identical for task sets with a few real-time tasks.

Another advantage of the proposed approach is its low computational complexity. This is very important for the large real-time task sets for which proposed algorithm took under a second to generate a near optimal solution. On the other hand, the optimal frequency assignment algorithm is considerably slower, almost unusable. Thus for large realtime task sets the proposed heuristic algorithm is the only realistic solution.
